newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia share rally seen hitting gold brick wall.
newsitem.headline: Australia share rally seen hitting gold brick wall.

text.p: The Australian share market's three month-long bull run, its longest and strongest in three years, appears to have hit a brick wall in the form of a five percent slump in the gold price, equity strategists said on Tuesday.

Australia's key All Ordinaries Index rose 17.8 percent to a record high of 2,757.9 between April 3 and July 3, fired by a surprise official cash rate cut, low inflation and expectations of a surge in economic growth and company profits.
But since that July 3 high, the index has fallen on three consecutive days by a total of 78.7 points or about three percent.

Ironically the trigger for the gold price slump and the subsequent equity market correction came from Australia's own central bank, which shocked gold traders early last Friday when it announced it had sold 167 tonnes or two-thirds of its gold.
Strategists said the index's 33.8 point fall to a close of 2,679.2 on Tuesday, its largest fall since April 1, confirmed the bull run had ended.
They predicted the market would at best plateau from here and may even correct another two or three percent.
But they said Australian shares remained well supported by projected earnings growth and any market correction would be measured.
"I don't think it's anything more serious than a natural correction," said HSBC James Capel Australia chief strategist Marcus Tuck.
"A big catalyst for it is the collapse in the gold price, but it was technically overdue anyway," he said.
Australia's gold share index has suffered a virtual meltdown, falling 18.6 percent in the last three days trade and wiping over A$2.5 billion (US$1.85 billion) from its market capitalisation.

Strategists said many institutional investors in particular had used the gold price fall as an excuse to ease up on the buying accelerator now their financial year to June 30 profits had been booked. Fund managers were expected to re-enter the market after a small correction and start hunting for bargains.
"The gold index has been the catalyst. I'm not sure that I'd be calling for a significant correction in our market," said Bankers Trust Australia equity strategist David Rees.
"I guess you could argue for a five percent overall correction. If it goes more than that I'd argue that you're in relatively cheap territory," he said.
Merrill Lynch Australia equity strategist John Banos said the bull run had now ended and he saw a basially flat market over the next three months to a year.
"A number of valuations were looking a little bit stretched, so it's good that we've had a bit of a correction. From here, we'd be saying there's a flat outlook," Banos said.
The key factors seen driving the size of the correction are the chances of a Reserve Bank rate cut and whether U.S. stocks will dive back 5-10 percent as expected to more realistic levels.
Strategists said they would be watching key local inflation and wages data on July 23 and July 24 respectively for pointers to another rate cut.

Australian shares would remain well supported while their price to earnings (P/E) ratios remained at their current levels of about 14.5 to 15 for industrial stocks and about 11 to 12 for resources stocks.
This compares with P/E ratios of about 20 for industrials on Wall St.
